guard: one persona-ownership predicate governs BOTH manager persona doors, fail-closed on ownerless files, with the spawn-door narrowing opt-in so an existing single-operator mesh is unaffected
why: The manager has two persona doors and only one of them was authorized. The WRITE door refused
to let a peer redefine a persona it did not own, and was fail-closed on ownerless files. The
SPAWN door checked nothing, so the same operator-written `deploy_runner` the write door
protected was launchable by any caller that named it — and ownerless, the write door's most
conservative case, was the spawn door's most permissive one.
E1 and E2 are the two halves of the rule. E1 makes ownerless files permissive, which is the
exact original inversion and the one a reader is most likely to call a cleanup ('no owner, no
restriction'). E2 drops the cross-owner check while leaving ownerless fail-closed, so the
headline case still refuses and only a peer-vs-peer cell can see it.
E3 removes the admin escape hatch. It is the mutation that makes the suite prove the rule has a
deliberate operator path rather than merely refusing a lot.
E4 flips the DEFAULT to the narrow setting. Every ownership cell stays green under it — the rule
is untouched — and it would still break every existing single-operator mesh on upgrade by
refusing its own catalog. That is the same default-allow trap as the DM work, and it is
invisible to any cell that only tests the predicate.
E5 attacks the anti-drift cell itself: it re-inlines the comparison at the spawn door while
leaving the predicate in place, which is precisely how the two copies would diverge later. If
that cell cannot see a second copy appear, it is decoration.
SPECIFIER BOUNDARY. The suite imports the manager by relative source path (../src/manager.js)
and runs under tsx, so the mutated file is the file that executes; the source-structure cells
read that same file from disk. No build stands between the mutation and the assertion.

mutations.name: E1 an ownerless (operator) persona becomes permissive
mutations.expectRed: an OWNERLESS (operator/legacy) file is refused, named 'ownerless'
mutations.cell: an OWNERLESS (operator/legacy) file is refused, named 'ownerless'
mutations.note: The exact inversion the spawn door shipped with. Reads as a tidy-up ('no owner means no restriction'), and re-opens deploy_runner to every participant.

mutations.name: E2 the cross-owner check is dropped, ownerless left fail-closed
mutations.note: Leaves the headline ownerless case still refusing, so only a peer-vs-peer cell can catch it. E1 cannot stand in for this and vice versa.

mutations.name: E3 the operator escape hatch is removed
mutations.expectRed: an ADMIN may act on another's persona
mutations.cell: an ADMIN may act on another's persona
mutations.note: Proves the rule has a deliberate operator path, rather than the suite merely rewarding refusal.

mutations.name: E4 the DEFAULT flips to the narrow setting
mutations.note: Every predicate cell stays green — the rule is untouched. This is the upgrade-path trap: a single-operator mesh would start refusing its own catalog, and only a cell that asserts the DEFAULT can see it.

mutations.name: E5 the spawn door re-inlines the rule beside the predicate
mutations.find: const denial = personaOwnerDenial(def, spawner ?? "", opts.adminTier ?? false);
mutations.replace: const denial = def.owner !== spawner ? "not-owner" as const : undefined;
mutations.expectRed: the predicate is CALLED at exactly two doors (write + spawn)
mutations.cell: the predicate is CALLED at exactly two doors (write + spawn)
mutations.note: The predicate still exists and the write door still calls it, so every behavioural cell about the RULE stays green. Only the structural cells see the second copy appear — which is the whole point of having them.
